title: Multisensory Virtual Reality for Human-Built Environment Interactions
author: Lyu, Globa, et al.
materials: The hardware set-up of the dynamic airflow simulation consists of the assembly of the Wind Control Module, fans, and VR headset. The Wind Control Module is made of Arduino UNO Rev3 (microcontroller), solderless breadboard (circuit prototyping board), infrared LED receiver, infrared transmitting LED and resistor. It works as a digitally programed remote control for the operation of the fan to simulate the turbulence characteristics of natural wind. Two functions are achieved, the ability to receive IR signal from the fan's original remote controller to configure the Arduino Uno Rev3, and the ability to send IR signal to control the fan. Firstly, a series circuit was designed to connect the infrared LED receiver, infrared transmitting LED and the Arduino Rev 3 microcontroller with the Arduino jumper wires (Fig. 3). Wind Control Module can be connected to the PC from its USB connector so that it can get powered (5v) and receive signal from the serial port in the PC. The infrared transmitting LED has a limited viewing angle (normally 30° - 40°), so during operation it should point towards the location of IR sensor on the fan (Fig. 4).Fig. 3Schematic Diagram for Connections in Wind Control Module. Note: Components in this figure are not on the same scale. Elements are resized to show more details.Fig 3Fig. 4Wind Control Module Prototype.Fig 4
(1)Determine fan's location in relation to the user.

The Sunlight Control Module works as a digitally controlled power relay for the operation of the halogen lamps. Instead of using the Solderless Breadboard, prototyping shields were used to provide a permanent configuration of the circuit. In addition, the control module was mounted into a sealed polycarbonate box which has openings for connections to computer and power source. Therefore, the need for physical access to the circuit can be minimized for electrical safety (as direct current is controlled via this module). No resistor is added in the circuit because the power relay contains one. The capacity of the power relay (10Amp 250 Volts, capable of supporting 2500 W external device) to control the halogen lamps was checked (Fig. 5, Fig. 6).(1)Connect the power relay to the Arduino prototyping board shield with soldering. Note: Connect S to any of the digital pin in the prototyping shield (in the example, pin 12 was used), “+” to the 5 V pin, and “-” to the Ground pin.(2)Create openings in the Sealed Polycarbonate Enclosure for the power socket boards, power plug and USB connection. Fix the power socket boards on to the box.(3)Connect the power relay, power socket boards and power plug with electrical cable. Note: Connect the “C” (Common) end of power relay to the Active wire of the power plug, “NO” (Normally Open) end of the power relay to the Active Terminal of the power socket, the Earth wire of the power plug to the Earth Terminal of the power socket and the Neutral wire of the power plug to the Neutral Terminal of the power socket.(4)The Arduino prototyping board shield needs to be plugged onto the Arduino Uno Rev3.(5)The Arduino Uno Rev3 with the prototyping shield plugged should be mounted onto the base of the protection box.(6)Connect Sunlight Control Module to the PC via USB, to the halogen lamps and to Direct Current supply.(7)The location of the halogen lamps in relation to the VR user needs to be determined based on the specific requirements. Radiation flux density may be measured for this purpose.Fig. 5Schematic Diagram for Connections in Sunlight Control Module. Note: Components in this figure are not on the same scale. steps.title: Assemble Wind Control Module
steps.instruction: Build the wind‑control hardware using an Arduino UNO Rev3, a solderless breadboard, an infrared LED receiver, an infrared transmitting LED with its resistor, and connect the fan’s IR sensor; power the module via USB (5 V) and ensure the transmitting LED points toward the fan’s IR sensor (≈30°‑40° viewing angle).

substeps.instruction: Place the infrared LED receiver, infrared transmitting LED, and resistor on a solderless breadboard and wire them to the Arduino UNO Rev3 using jumper wires (IR receiver to pin 8, transmitting LED to a digital output pin).
Connect the Arduino UNO Rev3 to the PC with a USB cable for power (5 V) and serial communication.
Mount the assembled circuit (the Wind Control Module) so that the transmitting LED faces the fan’s IR sensor during operation.

steps.title: Program Arduino for IR Control
steps.instruction: Upload two Arduino IDE sketches (IR signal receiver and IR signal sender) to the Arduino UNO Rev3, then record the fan remote’s encoded serial numbers for later use.

substeps.instruction: Connect the Arduino UNO Rev3 to the PC via USB.
Place Types.h, the IR‑receiver sketch, and the IR‑sender sketch in the same folder.
Open the IR‑receiver sketch in the Arduino IDE and upload it to the board.
Open the Serial Monitor (Tools → Serial Monitor).
In the Serial Monitor, type “r” and press Enter to activate the receiver function.
Point the fan’s original remote at the IR receiver and press the ON/OFF button; the serial number displayed is the encoded command for that function.
Repeat the previous two steps for each remote function (e.g., fan speed up and down) to collect all serial numbers.
Upload the IR‑sender sketch to the Arduino UNO Rev3.
Test a command by typing “s” followed by the recorded serial number and ending with “0” (e.g., s1230) to send the IR signal.

steps.title: Calibrate Fan and Create Airflow Commands
steps.instruction: Determine the fan’s position relative to the VR user with an anemometer, match measured velocities to target airflow levels, and translate those levels into Inc() and Dec() commands for Unity.

substeps.instruction: Place the fan at a provisional distance from the VR user.
Use an anemometer to measure air velocity at the fan’s maximum and minimum speeds.
Adjust the fan‑to‑user distance until the measured maximum velocity equals the desired maximum target airflow (m s⁻¹).
If the minimum target velocity cannot be reached, plan to add additional fans.
Convert the target airflow range into discrete velocity levels that correspond to fan speed steps.
Map each level change to Unity C# functions Inc() (increase) and Dec() (decrease); e.g., moving from level 1 to level 4 in one second requires three Dec() calls.
Record the sequence of Inc() and Dec() calls for each airflow profile.

steps.title: Integrate Wind Control into Unity
steps.instruction: Create Unity objects and scripts to send the recorded IR commands to the Arduino during VR runtime, and define wind zones that trigger those commands.

substeps.instruction: In Unity, create an empty GameObject named “Wind” and attach the supplied Wind Script component.
In the Wind Script inspector, fill the Serial Port Name (e.g., COM3) and enter all fan‑operation serial numbers obtained earlier.
Copy the airflow‑profile command sequences from the previous step into the wind‑profile function inside the Wind Script; create additional wind‑profile functions if multiple profiles are needed.
Create GameObjects representing microclimatic wind zones; add a Box Collider or Mesh Collider as appropriate, and attach the supplied Wind Zone script to each.
For each zone, assign the corresponding wind‑profile function in the script so that entering the zone triggers the profile.
Add a Capsule Collider (two half‑spheres joined by a cylinder) and a Rigidbody component to the VR avatar (XR Rig). Enable Collider.isTrigger and set Rigidbody.isKinematic.
Use Unity’s OnTriggerEnter to call the wind‑profile function when the avatar enters a wind zone, and OnTriggerExit to call CloseFan when it leaves.

steps.title: Assemble Sunlight Control Module
steps.instruction: Build a digitally controlled power‑relay circuit for halogen lamps using an Arduino prototyping shield, a 10 A / 250 V relay (2500 W rating), and mount everything in a sealed polycarbonate enclosure.

substeps.instruction: Solder the 10 A / 250 V power relay onto the Arduino prototyping shield; connect the relay’s “S” pin to any digital pin (example: pin 12), “+” to the 5 V pin, and “‑” to GND.
Drill openings in the sealed polycarbonate box for the power socket board, power plug, and USB cable; secure the socket board inside the box.

Wire the relay to the power plug and socket board: connect the relay’s Common (C) to the active wire of the plug, the Normally Open (NO) to the active terminal of the socket, the plug’s Earth wire to the socket’s Earth terminal, and the plug’s Neutral wire to the socket’s Neutral terminal.
Plug the prototyping shield onto an Arduino UNO Rev3.
Mount the Arduino UNO with the shield inside the base of the polycarbonate enclosure.
Connect the Sunlight Control Module to the PC via USB, to the halogen lamps, and to a DC power supply.
Determine the halogen‑lamp positions relative to the VR user; optionally measure radiation flux density for precise placement.

steps.title: Program Arduino for Sunlight Control
steps.instruction: Upload the Heatlamp‑Arduino script that reads serial characters and toggles the relay via digitalWrite to control halogen lamps.

substeps.instruction: Open the Heatlamp‑arduino‑script in the Arduino IDE.
The script uses Serial.readBytesUntil() to receive characters from the PC.

Define lamp‑operation modes with digitalWrite(): sending character “O” writes HIGH to the relay pin (opens the circuit for five lamps), sending other defined characters writes LOW (closes the circuit).
Upload the script to the Arduino UNO Rev3.

steps.title: Integrate Sunlight Control into Unity
steps.instruction: Create Unity objects and scripts that send serial commands to the Sunlight Control Module, and set up zones that trigger shaded, partially shaded, or sunlit conditions.

substeps.instruction: Create an empty GameObject named “Sunlight” and attach the supplied Artificial Sun Script component.
In the script inspector, enter the USB serial port name (e.g., COM1) as shown in Windows Device Manager.
Create GameObjects for each sunlight condition zone; add a Box Collider or Mesh Collider as needed, and attach the corresponding scripts: TriggerSunlit, TriggerShade, and TriggerPartialShade.
If a zone has an irregular shape, model a 3D mesh, import it into Unity, and add a Mesh Collider.
Drag the Sunlight GameObject into the “Artificial Sun” field of each zone script so that the zone can call the appropriate serial command (e.g., “C” to turn off two lamp sets).
Add a Capsule Collider and Rigidbody (isTrigger = true, isKinematic = true) to the VR avatar (XR Rig) as described in the wind‑control step.
